Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 1:

﴿Those are the verses of the Qur'an and of a clear Book.﴾ The conjunction of "Book" with "Qur'an" is like the conjunction of attributes with one another, even though the thing described is one.
﴿Guidance and good tidings﴾ is in the accusative case (naṣb) as a verbal noun (maṣdar), or in the nominative case (raf') as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtada').

﴿And they, in the Hereafter, they are certain﴾. This sentence may be taken as coordinated, so that it is the remainder of the relative clause (ṣila) of "those who", or it may be taken as a new, independent sentence, and the relative clause is complete before it. Al-Zamakhshari preferred this latter view.

﴿يَعْمَهُونَ﴾ meaning they are bewildered. ﴿سُوۤءُ ٱلْعَذَابِ﴾ meaning the worst of punishment. This refers to the punishment in this world, which is killing on the Day of Badr. It is possible that it means the punishment of the Hereafter, but the first view is more likely correct, because He mentioned the verse after it. ﴿لَتُلَقَّى ٱلْقُرْآنَ﴾ meaning you are given the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 7–8:

﴿Anastu﴾ (I have perceived) is mentioned in Ta-Ha [20:10], and likewise "qabas" (a burning brand) in Ta-Ha [20:10]. "Al-shihab" (the flame) means the star; the qabas is compared to it. It is also recited with the idafa (construct) of shihab to qabas, and with tanwin (nunation), in which case it is either a substitution (badal) or a qualifier (sifa). If it is asked: how does he say here ﴿sa-ataikum﴾ (I will bring you), while in the other place it is ﴿la'allli ataikum﴾ (perhaps I will bring you) [Ta-Ha: 10; al-Qasas: 29]? And what is the difference between hope (tarajji) and certainty (taswiq), since taswiq is certain to occur, unlike hope? The answer is that the one who hopes may say "it will be such-and-such" when his hope is strong. ﴿Tastalun﴾ (you may warm yourselves) means: you warm yourselves at the fire against the cold. Its measure is tafta'alun, and it is derived from salla bil-nar (he was exposed to the fire); the ta' has become a ta' (emphatic) in place of the ta' of the tafa'ul pattern. ﴿An bujika man fi al-nar﴾ (that blessed is whoever is in the fire): ﴿an﴾ is explanatory (mufassira); ﴿bujika﴾ is from al-barakah (blessing); and ﴿man fi al-nar﴾ means: whoever is in the place of the fire. ﴿Wa-man hawlaha﴾ (and whoever is around it): meaning, whoever is around its place; he intends the angels present and Musa, peace be upon him. Al-Zamakhshari said: the apparent meaning is that it is general, covering everyone who was in that land, and in that valley and what surrounded it of the land of al-Sham. ﴿Wa-subhana Allah﴾ (and glory be to Allah) may be part of what was said in the call to Musa, peace be upon him, or it may be a new (independent) statement. In both cases it is intended to declare Allah free of what might occur to the listener's mind regarding the meaning of the call, or regarding His saying ﴿bujika man fi al-nar﴾, because the meaning is "he was called: that blessed is whoever is in the fire," since some people said about it what it is obligatory to declare Allah free of.

﴿And cast down your staff﴾. This clause is joined (ma'tuf) to his saying ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, because the meaning leads to: ﴿Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾, and that ﴿cast down your staff﴾. Both are an explanation (tafsir) of the call (al-nida'). ﴿As if it were a jann﴾. The jann is the snake. It was said: it is the small snake. On this view a difficulty arises from his saying ﴿and behold, it was a thu'ban (a large serpent)﴾ [al-A'raf 107; al-Shu'ara' 32]. The answer is that it was a thu'ban in its bulk and a jann in the speed of its movement. ﴿And did not turn back﴾: did not return or did not look back. ﴿Except one who did wrong﴾: this is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), its sense being: but whoever among the rest of mankind did wrong, not the messengers. It was said that it is a connected exception (istithna' muttasil) on the view that sins are permissible for them, but this is far-fetched, because the sound view is that they are protected from sins (ma'sumun). Moreover, calling them wrongdoers is a grave matter on the view that sins are permissible for them. ﴿Has replaced evil with good﴾: that is, did righteous deeds. ﴿In your bosom﴾: mentioned in Ta-Ha [22]. ﴿Among nine signs﴾ is connected to his saying "cast" and "insert": its sense is: We shall make that easy for you as part of a group of nine signs. The nine signs have been mentioned in al-Isra' [101]. ﴿To Pharaoh﴾ is connected to a verb omitted that the context requires, its sense being: go with the nine signs to Pharaoh. ﴿Visible﴾: that is, evident and clear in indication. The seeing (al-ibsar) has been ascribed to them figuratively (majaz), while in reality it belongs to the one who contemplates them. ﴿And their souls were convinced of them﴾: meaning they denied them while they were certain that they were the truth, so their disbelief was obstinacy, and for this reason He said of it ﴿wrongfully and haughtily﴾ (zulman). The waw in it is the circumstantial waw (waw al-hal), and qad is implied after it: "they had exalted themselves", meaning they became arrogant.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 16–17:

﴿And Sulayman inherited from Dawud﴾: that is, he inherited from him prophethood, knowledge and kingship. ﴿We have been taught the speech of the birds﴾: that is, we understood from the sounds of the birds the meanings that are in their souls. ﴿And we have been given of everything﴾: the generality of its meaning is particularization (ʿumūm maʿnāhu al-khuṣūṣ), and what is intended by this expression is abundance, like your saying: "So-and-so is sought by everyone." And his saying "we have been taught" and "we have been given" may intend himself and his father, or himself alone in a manner of magnification, since he was a king. ﴿And for Sulayman were gathered his armies﴾: people have differed greatly over the number of Sulayman's armies; we have left aside mentioning it because it is not authentic. ﴿So they are held in check﴾: that is, they are restrained, and their first is driven back to their last. Every king or ruler必 has a guard (waza, pl. wazaʿa) who repel the people.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 18–19:

﴿Until, when they came upon the valley of the ants﴾ The apparent meaning is that Sulayman and his soldiers were walking on the ground, or riding, until the ants became frightened of them. It is also possible that they were on the throne (al-kursi) carried by the wind, and the ant sensed their descent into the valley of the ants. ﴿A certain ant said﴾ The naml (ant) is an animal, or rather an insect, that is shrewd and has a strong sense of perception. It stores its food, and it splits a grain into two halves so that it will not sprout. It splits a coriander seed (kusbara) into four pieces, because it would sprout if split into two. Because of the acuteness of its perception, it spoke these words. It is narrated that Sulayman heard her speech, though there was a distance of three miles between him and her. Human beings cannot hear this, except one whom God has singled out for that. ﴿Enter﴾ She addressed them as rational beings, because she commanded them with what rational beings are commanded. ﴿Let not Sulayman and his soldiers crush you﴾ This may be a response to the command, or a prohibition in place of a command, since the meanings are close. ﴿While they do not perceive﴾ The pronoun refers to Sulayman and his soldiers, and the meaning is an excuse on their behalf: if they had perceived the ants, they would not have crushed them. ﴿So he smiled, laughing﴾ He smiled for one of two reasons: one, his joy at what God had granted him; and the other, the ant's praise of him and his soldiers. Her saying "while they do not perceive" is a description of them as possessing piety and caution against harming living creatures.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 20:

﴿And he inspected the birds﴾. The scholars differed over the meaning of his inspecting the birds. It was said: this was out of his concern for the affairs of his kingdom. It was also said: because the birds used to shade him, and the hoopoe (al-Hudhud) was absent, so the sun reached him from its place. ﴿Or is he among the absent?﴾ The particle "am" here is munqati'ah (disjunctive, meaning "rather"). He looked at the place of the hoopoe and did not see it. ﴿He said: "Why is it that I do not see the hoopoe?"﴾ That is, "I do not see it," and perhaps it is present but something screens it from view. Then he knew that it was absent, and so he announced that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 22:

﴿فَمَكَثَ﴾ means he remained, stayed. The vowel of the kaf may be read with a fatha or a damma: ASIM read it with a fatha, while the rest read it with a damma. The verb may be understood as referring back to Sulayman, peace be upon him, or to the hoopoe (al-Hudhud), and the latter is more apparent. ﴿غَيْرَ بَعِيدٍ﴾ means a short time, a near period. ﴿أَحَطتُ﴾ means I have encompassed knowledge of what you have not known. ﴿مِن سَبَإٍ﴾ means a tribe from among the Arabs; their ancestor by whom they are known is Saba ibn Yashjub ibn Ya'rub ibn Qahtan. Whoever leaves it without nunation (Saba) intends the group (al-hayy) or the forefather, and whoever does not give it nunation intends the tribe or the town; and it was also read with sukun, Saba, to avoid a succession of vowels. On the reading with tanwin, the phrase "min Saba' bi-naba'" contains a kind of rhetorical embellishment of the badi' type, namely paronomasia (tajnis).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 23–24:

﴿I found a woman ruling over them﴾. The woman is Bilqis, daughter of Sharahil. Her father was king of Yemen, and he had no child other than her, so after him she gained control of the kingdom. The pronoun in "ruling over them" refers to Saba', and they are her people. ﴿of everything﴾: this is a general expression intended in a specific sense, referring to what a king needs. ﴿And she has a great throne﴾: this means the seat of her kingship. Some scholars paused at "throne" and then began with ﴿great﴾, and the sentence was taken as: ﴿I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah﴾ [with "great" as the predicate of "throne"]. This is an error, and what led them to it was the desire to avoid describing her throne as great.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 25:

﴿أَلاَّ يَسْجُدُواْ للَّهِ﴾ [Alla yasjudu lillah: "that they should not prostrate to Allah"]. Is this part of the speech of the hoopoe (al-Hudhud) or part of the speech of Allah? The majority of reciters read "ألاَّ" with the shadda (alla). The "أن" (an) is in a position of accusative (nasb) as a complement (badal) of their deeds, or it is in a position of genitive (khafd) as a substitute (badal) for "al-sabil" (the way). Or the estimate (taqdir) is: "لا يهتدون لأن يسجدوا" (they are not guided so that they prostrate), with the lam deleted and "لا" added. Al-Kisa'i read "ألا يا اسجدوا" with the lightening (takhfif), where "لا" is an interjection particle of alerting (harf tanbih), and the "ya" is a particle of calling (harf nida'), so it is stopped upon with an alif, on the estimate of "يا قوم" (O people), and then one begins with "اسجدوا" (prostrate). ﴿يُخْرِجُ ٱلْخَبْءَ﴾ [Yukhriju al-khab'a: "He brings forth the hidden"]. In language, "al-khab'" means the hidden. It was said that its meaning here is the unseen (al-ghayb). It was also said: He brings forth the plants from the earth. The wording encompasses everything hidden, and Ibn 'Abbas interpreted it that way.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 28:

﴿Then withdraw from them﴾ meaning: move aside to a nearby place so that you can hear what they say. It is related that he (the messenger) entered upon her through a window (kawwa), threw the letter to her, and then hid himself in the window. It was also said: the intended sense is "Look at what they return with; withdraw from them," and this is of the inverted construction (al-maqlub), but the first is better. ﴿What they return with﴾ comes from the phrase "some of them return the word to others" (yarji'u ba'duhum ila ba'd al-qawl).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 29–34:

﴿She said: "O chiefs!"﴾ Before this statement there is an omitted part, its implied meaning being: the hoopoe cast the letter to her, and she read it, then she gathered the people of her kingdom and said to them: "O chiefs! ﴿Indeed, a noble letter﴾" She described it as noble because it is from Solomon, or because it contains the name of God, or because it is sealed, as in the hadith: "The nobility of a letter is its seal." ﴿It is from Solomon﴾ This may be the actual text of the letter, which began with the address, or it may be her own words, informing them that the letter is from Solomon. ﴿And come to me in submission﴾ This may mean submitting in obedience, that is, "surrendering," or it may mean entering into Islam. ﴿Possessors of strength﴾ This may mean strength of bodies, or strength of kingdom and numbers. ﴿And thus do they act﴾ This is from the words of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, confirming her statement, so it is stopped at what precedes it; or it is from the words of Bilqis, emphasizing the meaning she intended, and she means: "Thus do these people act toward us."

﴿And indeed I am sending a gift to them﴾. She said to her people: "I will test this man with a gift of precious wealth. If he is a worldly king, wealth will please him. But if he is a prophet, wealth will not please him; what pleases him is our entry into his religion." So she sent him a great gift, whose description people have related, but we have abridged its description because it is not authentic.

"Do you provide me with wealth?" — a rebuke for the gift, because God has made him independent of it through what He has given him. "Rather, you rejoice in your gift." That is, you are in need of it, so you rejoice in it, whereas I am not like that.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 38:

﴿He said, "O assembly, which of you will bring me her throne before they come to me in submission?"﴾ The speaker is Sulayman, and "al-Mala'" (the assembly, the chiefs) is a group of jinn and humans. He sought her throne before they came to him in submission because it had been described to him as great, so he wanted to take it before they embraced Islam, so that their embracing Islam would prevent the taking of their wealth. Accordingly, "muslimin" (in submission) here means entering the religion of Islam. It has also been said: he sought her throne before they came to him in submission in order to display to them his power, so "muslimin" here means "obedient" (munqadin).

﴿A powerful jinn (ʿifrīt) said﴾. It is reported on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih that the name of this ʿifrīt was Kawzan. ﴿Before you rise from your place﴾, meaning before you rise from the place of judgment. He used to sit from the morning until noon. It was also said that the meaning is: before you rise from your sitting to a standing position.

﴿قَالَ ٱلَّذِي عِندَهُ عِلْمٌ مِّنَ ٱلْكِتَابِ﴾ "The one who had knowledge from the Scripture said." He is Asaf ibn Barkhiya, a righteous man from the Children of Israel who knew the Greatest Name of God (ism Allah al-a'zam). It is also said that he was al-Khidr, and it is said that he was Jibril (Gabriel). The first view is the best known. It is also said that he was Sulayman (Solomon), but this is far-fetched. ﴿آتِيكَ بِهِ﴾ "I will bring it to you," in both places. The phrase may be a standalone verb, or an active participle (ism al-fa'il). ﴿قَبْلَ أَن يَرْتَدَّ إِلَيْكَ طَرْفُكَ﴾ "before your glance returns to you." Al-tarf means the eye. On this reading the meaning is: before you close your eye, if you look at something. It is also said that al-tarf means the movement of the eyelids when one looks. ﴿فَلَمَّا رَآهُ مُسْتَقِرّاً عِندَهُ﴾ "So when he saw it placed firmly beside him." It is said that there is an omitted element here, its estimated form being: "Then came the one who had with him knowledge from the Scripture, concerning her throne." The meaning of mustaqirran ʿindahu (مُسْتَقِرّاً عِندَهُ) is that it is present and established with him. This is not the mustaqarr (مستقر, the stable place) that the grammarians (al-nahwiyyun) posit as the governing element of prepositional phrases (al-majrurat), contrary to those who understood it that way. ﴿يَشْكُرُ لِنَفْسِهِ﴾ "...whoever is grateful, is grateful only for his own benefit." That is, the benefit of gratitude returns to himself.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 41:

﴿He said: "Disguise her throne for her"﴾ Tankir (disguising) means altering its description and concealing part of it. It was also said: it means adding to it and subtracting from it. By this he intended to test her intellect and understanding. ﴿"Will she be guided?"﴾ This may mean: will she be guided to recognising her throne, or to answering about it if she is asked, or to faith.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 42:

﴿So when she came, it was said: "Is your throne like this?"﴾ Her throne had already been brought to Solomon before her, and he ordered that it be altered in appearance, and that she be asked: "Is your throne like this?" That is, "Is your throne something like this?" so that she would not realize that it was her own. She answered him with the words: ﴿"It is as if it were it"﴾, answering the question without saying "It is it," avoiding a lie, or making a definite claim where there is room for doubt. ﴿"And we had been given knowledge before her, and we had submitted"﴾ These are the words of Solomon and his people, spoken when they saw that she had become a believer; they said this in acknowledgment of God's blessing upon them, in that He gave them knowledge before Bilqis and guided them to Islam before her. The sentence is joined to an omitted statement, and its meaning is: "She has submitted and has known the oneness of God and the truth of prophethood, and we were given knowledge before her."

{And what she used to worship besides Allah had barred her (from faith)}. This may be the speech of Sulayman and his people, or the speech of Allah the Exalted. And "mā kānat taʿbudu" may be the subject (fāʿil) or the object (mafʿūl) of the verb. If it is the subject, the meaning is: what she used to worship besides Allah barred her from worshipping Allah and entering Islam up to this time. If it is the object, then the preposition has been dropped, and the meaning is: Allah or Sulayman barred her from what she used to worship besides Allah, so she entered Islam.

The palace (al-sarh) in the language means a palace, and it was said that it means the courtyard of a house. It is related that Sulayman, before her arrival, ordered for her a palace to be built on her route, made of white glass. He caused water to flow beneath it and placed in it sea creatures, fish and others. He set his throne in its middle and sat upon it. When she saw it, she thought it was a pool (lujja), and lujja is gathered water like the sea. So she uncovered her shins in order to enter it, as she had been commanded to enter.

It is also related that the jinn disliked Sulayman's marriage to her, so they said to him: "Her intellect is deficient, and her leg is like a donkey's hoof." So he tested her intellect by altering the throne, and found her intelligent. He tested her leg with the palace, and when she uncovered her shins, he found her to have the most beautiful shins of people. So he married her and confirmed her in her kingdom in Yemen, and he would visit her once every month. It was also said that he kept her with him in al-Sham.

﴿He said: "Indeed, it is a palace paved smooth, made of glass."﴾ When she thought the palace was a body of water and uncovered her shins to enter the water, Sulayman said to her: "It is a palace paved smooth (mumarrad)." Al-mumarrad means smooth, and it was also said to mean long. Al-qawarir is the plural of qarura, which is a glass bottle.

﴿She said: "My Lord, I have wronged myself"﴾, meaning by her disbelief previously, ﴿"and I have submitted with Sulayman to Allah, the Lord of the worlds."﴾ This is a kind of tajnis (paronomasia, a rhetorical play on similar-sounding words).

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 45–47:

﴿فَرِيقَانِ يَخْتَصِمُونَ﴾ "Two groups who dispute." The two groups are those who believed and those who disbelieved; their "disputing" (ikhtisam) is their difference of opinion and their argument over the religion.

﴿لِمَ تَسْتَعْجِلُونَ﴾ "Why do you seek to hasten?" That is: why do you seek punishment before mercy, or disobedience before obedience?

﴿قَالُواْ ٱطَّيَّرْنَا بِكَ﴾ "They said: We consider you a bad omen." That is: we take you as an evil omen (tatayyur, "augury"), and they had been afflicted by drought.

﴿قَالَ طَائِرُكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ﴾ "He said: Your omen is with Allah." That is: the cause from which your good or evil comes is with Allah; it is His decree and His destiny. This is a rebuttal of them in their taking omens, and of their attributing the drought that befell them to Salih, peace be upon him.

**[27:48]** ﴿And there were in the city﴾ meaning the city of Thamud, ﴿who spread corruption in the land﴾. It was said: they used to clip gold and silver coins (dinar and dirham), but the word "corruption" (fasad) is more general than that.

﴿They said: "Swear to one another by Allah"﴾, meaning they swore by Allah. It was also said that this is a past-tense verb (tqasamu), but that is weak. The correct view is that it is an imperative (taqasamu), said by some of them to others, and they bound themselves by it.

﴿"We will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾, meaning we will surely kill him and his family at night. This is the act they pledged to carry out.

﴿Then we will surely say to his heir: "We did not witness the destruction of his family"﴾, meaning we will disclaim his blood if we are asked about it by his heir. "Destruction" (mahlik) may be a verbal noun, a time noun, or a place noun. If it is asked: their saying "We did not witness the destruction of his family" implies disavowing the blood of his family, not disavowing his own blood, the answer is in three ways. First, they meant "We did not witness his destruction or the destruction of his family," and "his destruction" was omitted because of the indication of their saying "We will surely attack him and his family." Second, the "family" of a person may refer to him and them, as in His saying: "and We drowned the family of Pharaoh," meaning Pharaoh and his people. Third, they said "the destruction of his family" specifically so that they would be truthful, for they had witnessed both his destruction and his family's destruction together, and they intended an allusion in their speech so that they would not be lying.

**[27:49]** ﴿And indeed we are truthful﴾. It may be that their saying "And indeed we are truthful" was deception while they believed themselves liars. It may also be that they intended a kind of allusion, by which they would escape lying, which we have mentioned in the third answer regarding "the destruction of his family": that they intended to kill Salih and his family together, and then say, "We did not witness the destruction of his family alone," and "we are truthful in that," meaning they witnessed his destruction and his family's destruction together. Al-Zamakhshari also interpreted it this way.

Verse 51–58 commentary:

﴿That We destroyed them and their people﴾. It is related that the group who conspired together to kill Salih hid by night in a cave near his dwelling, so that they might come out from it to his house at night. A rock fell upon them and destroyed them. Then their people perished by the Blast (al-Sayha), and some of them did not know of the destruction of others. Salih and those who believed in him were saved. ﴿And you were watching﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that you perceive with your hearts that it is disobedience. It has also been said: you perceive with your eyes, because they used to uncover themselves while doing that, and none of them would conceal himself from another. It has also been said: you perceive the traces of the disbelievers before you and the punishment that befell them. ﴿They purify themselves﴾ and ﴿those who remained behind﴾ [al-Ghabirin]. ﴿And We rained﴾ [upon them a rain]: this has already been mentioned.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verses 59–61:

﴿Say: "All praise is for Allah, and peace be upon His servants whom He has chosen."﴾ Allah commanded His Messenger to recite the verses mentioned after this, because they are proofs of His oneness and His power, and to begin that with His praise and with peace upon those of His servants whom He has chosen, just as sermons, books and other works are begun in this way, seeking blessing through the mention of Allah. Ibn ʿAbbas said: By "His servants whom He has chosen" he means the Companions. But the wording includes the angels, the prophets, the Companions and the righteous. ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate (with Him)?﴾ This is in the form of a rebuttal of the polytheists, so the particle "khayr" (better), which is intended to express preference, was used to rebuke and reproach them, even though it is known that there is no good at all in what they associate with Allah. Then He established the proof against them that Allah is the One who created the heavens and the earth, and other things He mentioned up to the end of these verses. He followed each proof of them with His saying: ﴿Is there a god along with Allah?﴾ as an affirmation to them, that none has done all of that except Allah alone. Thus the proof was established against them by this, and in them are also blessings that must be thanked, so the proof was established by that as well. As for His saying ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate?﴾, "am" here is connective (muttasila ʿatifa), while "am" in the places after it is disconnected (munqatiʿa), meaning "bal" (rather) together with the hamza. ﴿A people who deviate⦆ means: they deviate from the truth and what is right, or they make equals to Allah, i.e., they set up for Him a counterpart and likeness. ﴿Firmly fixed mountains⦆ means the mountains. ﴿The two seas⦆ has been mentioned in Surat al-Furqan [25:53].

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 65:

﴿Say: None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except Allah﴾. This verse necessitates that Allah, exalted is He, alone possesses knowledge of the unseen, and that none other than Him knows it. For this reason, ʿĀ'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Whoever claims that Muhammad knows the unseen has greatly slandered Allah," and then she recited this verse. If it is said: The Prophet (ﷺ) used to report unseen matters, and that is counted among his miracles, the answer is: he (ﷺ) said, "I do not know the unseen except what Allah has taught me." If it is said: How is that, in light of what has appeared of the reports of soothsayers (kuhhān), astrologers (munajjimūn), and their like about hidden matters? The answer is: their reporting of that is based on weak conjecture or illusion, not on knowledge, and the verse only necessitates the negation of knowledge. It has also been said that the unseen in this verse refers to when the Hour will come, because the occasion of its revelation was that they asked about that, and for this reason He said: ﴿and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾. On this basis the first objection is dispelled. The second is that knowledge of the Hour is exclusive to Allah, exalted is He, according to His saying: ﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 63], and His saying (ﷺ): "There are five things that none knows except Allah," then he recited: ﴿Indeed, Allah has with Him knowledge of the Hour﴾ to the end of the surah. If it is said: How can it be said ﴿except Allah﴾ with the nominative (rafʿ) as a substitute (badal), and substitution is only valid if the exception is connected (istithnāʾ muttaṣil), and what follows illa must be of the same kind as what precedes it, whereas Allah, by consensus, is not among those in the heavens and the earth? For those who hold that Allah is in a direction (jiha) and place say that He is above the heavens and the earth, and those who deny a direction say that Allah is neither within them, nor above them, nor inside them, nor outside them. On this basis it is a disconnected exception (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ), so it should have been in the accusative (naṣb). The answer comes in four ways:

First: the substitution here came in the dialect of the Banu Tamim regarding substitution, even if disconnected, as in their saying: "There is no one in the house except a donkey" with the nominative, though the donkey is not of the category of "one." This is weak, because the Qur'an was revealed in the dialect of the Hijaz, not the dialect of the Banu Tamim.

Second: Allah is in the heavens and the earth by His knowledge, as He said: ﴿And He is with you wherever you are﴾ [al-Hadid: 4], meaning by His knowledge, so the substitution came according to this meaning. This is weak, because His saying ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ contains the particle "fi" (in) in its literal sense of enclosure, whereas in relation to Allah on this meaning it would be in a figurative sense, and it is not permissible, according to the scholars of verification (al-muḥaqqiqūn), to use one word in both its literal and figurative senses at the same time.

Third: His saying ﴿those in the heavens and the earth﴾ is intended to mean every existent thing, as if He had said "those in existence," so the exception is then connected, and the nominative as substitution is valid. He said ﴿those in the heavens and the earth﴾ following the pattern of Arabic speech: it is a specific expression intended to mean something more general than itself.

Fourth: the exception is connected, on the basis that "those in the heavens" is interpreted with regard to Allah, just as His saying is interpreted: ﴿Do you feel secure that He who is in the heaven...﴾ [al-Mulk: 16], and the hadith of the slave-girl and the like.

﴿and they do not perceive when they will be resurrected﴾, i.e., those in the heavens and the earth do not perceive when they will be resurrected, because knowledge of the Hour is among what Allah alone possesses. It is narrated that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that the Quraysh asked the Prophet (ﷺ): "When is the Hour?"

Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 66:

﴿Nay, their knowledge has been exhausted concerning the Hereafter﴾. The wazn (morphological pattern) of "ادّارك" (iddarak) is "تفاعل" (tafa'ala). Then the taa' was made sukun and the daal was assimilated (idghaam), and the hamzat al-wasl (alif of connection) was added. The meaning is that their knowledge about the Hereafter followed one another and reached its end, so that they disbelieve in it, or it reached the point where they do not know its time. It was also read as "أدرك" (adrak) with a hamzat al-qat' (hamza of cutting) on the pattern "أفعل" (af'ala). According to this reading the meaning is: "their knowledge of the Hereafter catches up," i.e., they know the truth in it, because at that time they witness the realities. So His saying "فِي ٱلآخِرَةِ" (in the Hereafter) on this reading is a time adverb (zarf), and on the first reading it carries the meaning of "الباء" (bi, "concerning"). "عَمُونَ" (ʿamūn) is the plural of "عَم" (ʿamm), and it is from the blindness of the hearts (ʿamā al-qulūb).

﴿radifa lakum﴾ means "followed you" (tabi'akum). The *lam* (the particle ل) is either extra (za'ida), or the verb is taken to include the sense of "drew near" (qariba), so it is construed with *lam*. The meaning of the verse is that they hastened the punishment by saying, "When is this promise?" So it was said to them: "It may be that some of the punishment you are hastening has drawn near to you," and that was their killing on the day of Badr.
The ha' in ﴿غَآئِبَةٍ﴾ (hidden thing) is for intensification (mubālagha): meaning, there is nothing in the utmost degree of concealment except that it is with God in a Book.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 27, verse 80:

﴿Indeed, you cannot make the dead hear﴾. He likened the one who neither hears nor understands to the dead, in that they do not hear even though they are alive. Then he likened them to the deaf and the blind, even though their senses are sound. He emphasized their not hearing with His saying ﴿when they turn away, retreating﴾, because the deaf person, when he turns away and moves far from the one calling him, his deafness increases and his not hearing becomes complete.

﴿And when the word is fulfilled against them﴾: that is, when the time of their punishment comes, which the eternal word from God regarding it contains, and that is His decree. The meaning is: when the Hour draws near, We will bring forth for them a beast from the earth. The emergence of the beast is among the signs of the Hour (ashrat al-sa'ah, the minor and major portents that herald the Hour). It is narrated that it will emerge from the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram), and it was said: from al-Safa. It was also said that its length is sixty cubits. It was said that it is the Jassasa (a creature mentioned in a hadith). ﴿It will speak to them﴾. It was said: it will speak to them about the falsehood of all religions except the religion of Islam. It was said: it will say to them, "Surely the curse of God is upon the wrongdoers." It is narrated that it will brand the disbeliever, cut off his nose, and blacken him, and it will whiten the face of the believer. ﴿Indeed, the people﴾: whoever reads it with a kasra on the hamza (إن) makes it the beginning of a new statement. Whoever reads it with a fatha (أن) makes it the object of tukallimuhum (it will speak to them): that is, it will say to them that the people were not certain of Our signs. Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ul min ajlih), its estimated form being tukallimuhum because the people were not certain, then the lam was elided. The phrase ﴿they were not certain﴾ may refer to the emergence of the beast, and to not being certain of the Hereafter and matters of religion. This last interpretation is the more apparent.

﴿So they will be driven﴾, meaning they will be driven forcefully. ﴿"What was it that you used to do?"﴾ Am is interrogative (*istifhamiyya*, meaning used to ask a question), and the sense is to establish the proof against them, as if it were said to them: if you have any deed or proof, then produce it. ﴿And the word will be fulfilled against them﴾, meaning the punishment is due against them, or the proof has been established against them. ﴿So they will not speak﴾. They are silent only because the proof has been established against them, and this is in some of the stations of the Resurrection. It has also been reported that they speak in other stations. ﴿To rest therein﴾, mentioned in Yunus [6]. ﴿When the Horn is blown﴾, mentioned in al-Kahf [99]. ﴿Except whom Allah wills﴾. It has been said: they are the martyrs. It has also been said: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil and 'Izra'il, peace be upon them. ﴿Humbled﴾, meaning abased and submissive.

﴿You think them solid﴾, that is, standing firm, ﴿but they pass away as clouds pass away﴾. This city (Makkah), the One Who has made it sacred. ... 

Let me translate properly:

"This city" — meaning Makkah. "The One Who has made it sacred" — i.e., He made it a sanctuary (ḥaram) and a place of safety, where no one fights and no one violates its sanctity. The making of it sacred is attributed here to Allah because it is by His decree and command. The Prophet ﷺ attributed it to Ibrahim (peace be upon him) in his saying: "Indeed, Ibrahim made Makkah sacred." This is because Ibrahim was the one who informed people of its sanctity, so there is no contradiction between the hadith and the verse. Another hadith has come stating that Makkah was made sacred by Allah on the day He created the heavens and the earth.

"And as for whoever strays, say: I am only one of the warners" — i.e., my duty is only to warn and to convey.

"He will show you His signs" — a warning of punishment that will compel them to recognize the signs of Allah, either in this world or in the Hereafter.

"He will show you His signs" — a warning of punishment that will compel them to recognize the signs of Allah, either in this world or in the Hereafter.
